newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Primagaz Q1 results hit by mild winter.
newsitem.headline: Primagaz Q1 results hit by mild winter.

text.p: Hungarian liquefied petroleum gas distributor Primagaz on Wednesday reported lower IAS operating profits and slightly firmer after-tax profits for the first quarter of 1997.

"Our figures declined due to warm weather (in late February and early March) but consumption in late March and in April brought this back to more or less normal," Zoltan Szemmelveisz, Primagaz's General Manager, told a news conference.
"In addition world market prices (for LPG) rose very substantially this winter," he added.

Primagaz, which has a 75 percent market share in Hungary, reported its IAS operating profits falling to 550 million forints in the first three months of 1997 from 622 million in the same period of 1996, while its sales rose to 5.525 billion forints from 4.688 billion.
The high world market price for LPG forced Primagaz to pay $250 per tonne -- the upper end of a price formula set in a 10-year deal with its supplier oil and gas company MOL -- since last November.

This deal says that if the upper end of the price formula prevails for three months -- and this happened in November, December and January -- the partners have to renegotiate the pricing formula and Primagaz had to accept a rise of $25.
"Since the 1st of February, the maximum price in our long-term deal (with MOL) rose to $275," Szemmelveisz said.
Nevertheless, the company boosted its after-tax profits marginally, to 394 million forints in the first three months of 1997 from 392 million in the same period of 1996.

Despite the lower operating profits Primagaz said the first quarter figures formed a good base for the business year. Szemmelveisz said the relatively cold weather in April and May, followed by at least average weather in autumn, should help the company's results.

Szemmelveisz said Primagaz had left its business plans unchanged for the year. "It's too early to speak about any amendments in our plans," he said, adding that current forecasts indicated sales volumes would be about as planned.

Asked about the company's dividend policy for 1997, Szemmelveisz said it was unchanged and Primagaz was aiming at paying 50 percent of its net income (according to Hungarian Accounting Standards) in dividends.
